nameStory: The 'beardtongue' name comes from a fuzzy, tongue-like projection (called a staminode) that sticks out from the flower's throat like a tiny beard. The 'long-sepal' part refers to the unusually long, pointed sepals - those green, leaf-like structures that form the outer part of the flower bud and remain visible at the base of the open flower.
description: Long-sepal beardtongue is a perennial wildflower that grows 2-3 feet tall with tubular, two-lipped flowers in shades of pink, purple, or white. The flowers cluster at the top of sturdy stems, creating an eye-catching display from late spring through summer. This relatively uncommon plant has smooth, lance-shaped leaves and a neat, upright growth habit that makes it look almost cultivated in the wild.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Tubular, two-lipped flowers about an inch long in pink, purple, or white, with a fuzzy 'tongue' visible in the throat; flowers cluster at stem tips and have a slightly sweet fragrance

idTips.label: Sepals
idTips.description: Unusually long, narrow, pointed sepals that extend well beyond the base of the flower tube - much longer than those of related beardtongues

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Smooth, lance-shaped leaves arranged in opposite pairs along the stem; leaves feel firm and slightly waxy to the touch

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Neat, upright perennial reaching 2-3 feet tall with multiple flowering stems arising from a basal rosette

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Small, egg-shaped capsules that split open to release tiny, angular seeds; capsules remain visible into fall

habitat: In New England, long-sepal beardtongue is extremely rare, found occasionally in open woodlands, woodland edges, and rocky slopes, often over limestone or calcium-rich soils. Look for it in partly sunny spots where the forest canopy is broken, particularly in areas with well-drained, alkaline soil conditions.

seasonality.spring: New growth emerges as a basal rosette of smooth leaves, with flowering stems beginning to develop in late spring.
seasonality.summer: Peak blooming period with showy clusters of tubular flowers that attract bees and butterflies; flowers continue through mid-summer.
seasonality.fall: Flowers fade and seed capsules mature and split open; leaves may turn yellowish before dying back.
seasonality.winter: Dies back completely to underground roots; no above-ground parts remain visible.

funFact: This plant is actually a relatively recent arrival to New England, having expanded its range northeastward from the Midwest and Upper South only in the early 20th century - making it one of the few native wildflowers that has naturally colonized new territory in modern times.
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with foxglove beardtongue, but long-sepal beardtongue has much longer, more prominent sepals extending from the flower base, and its flowers are typically more colorful (pink to purple) rather than the white of foxglove beardtongue. Memory trick: 'Long-sepal' has long sepals that you can actually notice!
contextualKnowledge: Despite being native to North America, this species is so rare in New England that many local botanists have never seen it in the wild - with only 3 recorded observations in the entire region, making any sighting truly special.
compareHints: Long-sepal beardtongue stands out from other New England beardtongues primarily by its dramatically longer sepals and typically more colorful flowers. While foxglove beardtongue has white flowers and short sepals, and hairy beardtongue is much smaller with fuzzy leaves, long-sepal beardtongue combines smooth foliage with showy pink-purple flowers and those distinctive elongated sepals.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among New England's beardtongues, foxglove beardtongue is the tallest and has the whitest flowers - hairy beardtongue has purple-pink flowers and fuzzy leaves, while pale beardtongue is much shorter with smaller, paler flowers.
Among New England's beardtongues, hairy beardtongue is distinguished by its noticeably fuzzy stems and smaller purple flowers.
Among New England's beardtongues, pale beardtongue stands out for its very light, almost ghostly flower color compared to the bright white foxglove beardtongue or the purple-pink hairy beardtongue.

Eastern gray beardtongue stands out from other New England beardtongues by its distinctly fuzzy, grayish leaves - foxglove beardtongue has smooth green leaves, while hairy beardtongue is much shorter and has purple flowers.
